{"source":"The archive keeps a copy of every published guide so readers can follow older links. When a guide changes, its old address points to the archived version rather than the latest one. This is intentional. A link in a training document should continue to show the instructions that were current when that document was written. People comparing an old procedure with today's procedure need to know which version they are reading, especially when the steps look nearly the same at first glance.

An archived page has a date below its title and cannot be edited. To find the current guide, use the blue Current version link at the top of the archived page. That link takes readers out of the archive and into the guide they should use now. The link is absent when a guide has been withdrawn without a replacement. In that situation, the archived page is a record of what was published, not an invitation to keep following those instructions. Staff answering a question should check whether a current version exists before sharing an archive link as advice.

If a current page is missing content, report the problem from that page. Reports sent from the archive are routed to a different queue, because they refer to a preserved version. Starting from the page with the problem helps the receiving team see which version needs attention. An archived copy itself cannot be edited to repair the current guide, even if the missing content is visible in that older copy.

Some staff have asked whether the archive is also a backup for drafts. It is not a way to recover an unpublished draft. Drafts are stored separately and may be deleted under the normal retention policy. The archive only holds guides that were published at least once. A draft that was never published will not appear there, no matter how complete it was when someone last worked on it.","candidate":"Archived guides: internal FAQ

**Why does the archive keep old copies of guides?**
The archive keeps a copy of every published guide so readers can follow older links. When a guide changes, its old address points to the archived version rather than the latest one.

**Is that a bug?**
It's intentional. A link in a training document should continue to show the instructions that were current when that document was written. People comparing an old procedure with today's procedure need to know which version they are reading, especially when the steps look nearly the same at first glance.

**How can I tell I'm on an archived page?**
An archived page has a date below its title and cannot be edited.

**How do I find the current guide?**
Use the blue Current version link at the top of the archived page. It takes readers out of the archive and into the guide they should use now.

**What if there's no Current version link?**
The link is absent when a guide has been withdrawn without a replacement. In that case, the archived page is a record of what was published, not an invitation to keep following those instructions. If you're answering a question, check whether a current version exists before you share an archive link as advice.

**The current guide is missing content. Where do I report it?**
Report the problem from the current page. Reports sent from the archive are routed to a different queue, because they refer to a preserved version. Starting from the page with the problem helps the receiving team see which version needs attention. You can't edit an archived copy to repair the current guide, even if the missing content is visible in that older copy.

**Is the archive a backup for drafts?**
No. It is not a way to recover an unpublished draft. Drafts are stored separately and may be deleted under the normal retention policy. The archive only holds guides that were published at least once. A draft that was never published will not appear there, no matter how complete it was when someone last worked on it.","objective":"Turn this into a clear internal FAQ about archived guides. Keep the distinction among old links, current guides, withdrawn guides, and unpublished drafts. Retain the report-routing detail.","deterministicFindings":[{"kind":"added_claim","severity":"warning","origin":"deterministic","message":"“FAQ” appears in the rewrite but not in your text.","candidate":"FAQ"},{"kind":"assertion_strength_changed","severity":"warning","origin":"deterministic","message":"The qualifier “some” was dropped, which generalises the claim.","source":"Some staff have asked whether the archive is also a backup for drafts.","candidate":"**Is the archive a backup for drafts?**"},{"kind":"added_claim","severity":"warning","origin":"deterministic","message":"Likely added content: 2 of 2 content words are not in the source.","candidate":"internal FAQ"}],"authorizedChanges":[],"voiceDeviations":[],"protectedPhrases":["into the guide","with the problem"]}

{"source":"We're preparing a note for teams that borrow the portable display kit. Right now the note tells people to return it to the usual place by the end of the day. That sounds simple until a team uses the kit for an evening event. The storage room may close before the event is over, so a borrower could be following the event plan and still be unable to make that deadline. The note should describe a return window that people can actually use.

The proposed rule is to return the kit by the following business day, when the storage room is open. The exact closing time of the room is not in this brief, and hours may differ by site. Please direct borrowers to check their site's posted storage-room hours instead of supplying a single clock time. The note should also avoid implying that every site opens at the same time. A borrower finishing an evening event needs to know the next step without guessing whether an after-hours return is expected.

Before returning the kit, staff should pack the display, stand, and two cables in its case. Listing the pieces matters because they are used together and can be separated during setup or packing. A quick check while closing the case will make it easier to tell the desk whether a part is missing. The note does not need a lengthy inventory procedure; it just needs a clear reminder of what belongs in the case.

If a cable is missing, staff should still return the kit by the stated window and report the missing part to the desk. They should not hold the rest of the kit while looking for the cable. The desk needs the report so the next borrower can be warned before planning to use it. Keep those two actions together in the note: return what is available, and tell the desk what is absent.","candidate":"Portable display kit: return and packing note

Please return the kit to the usual place by the following business day, when the storage room is open. Earlier guidance said to return it by the end of the day. That doesn't work for a team using the kit at an evening event, because the storage room may close before the event is over. A borrower could be following the event plan and still be unable to make that deadline.

Storage-room hours may differ by site. Check your site's posted storage-room hours. Don't assume every site opens at the same time. If your event ends in the evening, the next step is to return the kit the following business day. No after-hours return is expected.

Before returning the kit, pack the display, stand, and two cables in its case. {"source":"The purpose of the proposed equipment library is to support community groups that need tools occasionally but cannot justify buying them. The initial collection would include folding tables, portable display boards, and two battery-powered speakers. We have deliberately excluded items that require specialist training or expensive servicing.

Groups would book equipment through the community centre and collect it during staffed hours. A deposit would be required for the speakers, but not for tables or display boards. Deposits would be returned after a check on the next working day. This may be inconvenient for some borrowers, so the booking information must make the timing clear.

The pilot would operate for nine months. We would record bookings, late returns, repair costs, and requests for equipment we do not stock. Those records would help us decide whether to expand the collection. They would not measure the wider social benefit of the events at which equipment was used.

There is a risk that the service will become an additional administrative burden for reception staff. We propose reviewing workload after the first six weeks and shortening collection hours if necessary. The proposal depends on having enough staff time to run the pilot safely; a donated collection without that support would not be sufficient.","candidate":"The proposed equipment library would support community groups that need tools occasionally but cannot justify buying them.
